description: LifeGuard Orbit learns each crew member's personal baseline from wearable-type signals (heart rate, HRV, SpO2, skin temperature, activity, sleep), flags drift from that person's own normal, and raises graduated, explained alerts. Runs offline. Research prototype, not clinically validated; all crew data is simulated.
summary: On long missions, astronauts have to notice changes in their own health, often far from ground support. LifeGuard Orbit is an offline dashboard that learns each crew member's personal baseline from wearable-type signals: resting heart rate, HRV, SpO2, skin temperature, activity and sleep. It checks signal quality first, then scores drift from that person's own normal and raises graduated alerts (Info, Watch, Act). Each alert says why: which signals moved, by how much, and how reliable they are. It adds a body map linked to NASA Human Research Program risks, a daily check-in, and real NASA DONKI space-weather events as context only. This is a research prototype on simulated crew data. It is not clinically validated and not a diagnosis.
details:
What it does. LifeGuard Orbit helps a crew member answer one question each day: is anything drifting away from my normal, and what should I do about it? It shows four simulated crew members over a 42-day mission. Each has a mission dial (one segment per day, coloured by alert level), six signal charts with a personal-baseline band, an hourly trace, a clickable body map, a "What to do now" list, a mood/symptom/water check-in stored on the device, a routine with a wear streak, and an "Export ground packet" button. The packet is a JSON summary that can be sent when the comms window opens.

How it works.

1. Qualify: it counts wear coverage, rejects poor-contact SpO2 and loose-fit temperature readings, and withholds unstable nights. Missing data is never treated as normal.

2. Personalize: it takes the median and robust spread of each person's last 14 clean days. The first 7 days are for learning only. Alert days are left out of the baseline, so a slow drift can't become the new normal.

3. Score: each signal gets a directional robust z-score, weighted by signal quality. A leaky accumulator adds up sustained drift, sleep loss has its own accumulator, and alerts need several days of confirmation so a single odd night fades. A separate check catches slow drifts across several signals at once.

4. Alert: Info -> Watch -> Act, plus a check at night SpO2 <= 92% (MedlinePlus consumer guidance). Every alert lists the exact numbers behind it.

The guidance is deliberately conservative: re-measure, log symptoms, review hydration, sleep and workload, and at Act, contact the flight surgeon per mission protocol.

How we tested it (simulated data only). The simulator draws each person's normal from published ranges: AHA heart rate, Nunan 2010 HRV, MedlinePlus/FDA SpO2, Barger 2014 ISS sleep, and NASA's ~2 h/day of exercise. It adds day-to-day wander, charging gaps and loose-fit nights. It then plants test scenarios: infection-like drift, dehydration-like drift, sleep disruption, sensor dropout, and confounders (a heavy-exercise day, one bad night, a warm cabin). We tuned the thresholds on seeds 0-59 and report on 200 held-out simulated missions (seeds 1000-1199) with randomised onsets and strengths:

- 419 of 600 planted episodes detected (69.8%), with a median delay of 3 days after onset.

- By scenario: infection-like 92.0%, sleep disruption 69.5%, dehydration-like 48.0%.

- False alerts on 0.76% of negative crew-days.

- All 401 sensor-dropout days held as "no score".

- Look-alike days that triggered an alert: 40 of 1195 (single bad night 19/397). Our second engine version added multi-day confirmation and a slow-trend check; it cut these and more than doubled dehydration-like detection, at the cost of about one more day of median delay for infection-like and sleep scenarios (overall median unchanged at 3 days).

These numbers check the software on data we made ourselves. They are not medical accuracy.

Benefits. It works fully offline with no ground link. Each alert explains itself in plain numbers. It is honest about missing data and puts the person's own baseline ahead of population cut-offs. The same engine could run on a spacecraft, a station, a rover or a surface base.

What we hope to achieve. We want independent and clinical evaluation with qualified people and real, consented data. We'd also like to add blood pressure and glucose inputs and longer-term adaptation models.

Tools. Python 3 (standard library only) for the simulator, engine, evaluation and DONKI fetcher. HTML, CSS, SVG and vanilla JavaScript for the dashboard, with no frameworks, external fonts or images. pytest and Playwright with headless Chrome for the tests (21 tests passing).
dataRefs: NASA Human Research Program - Risks of Human Spaceflight
